lines.title: Welcome to the lot
lines.text: Welcome to the parking lot. In the next two minutes, you will see how programs in a computer can get completely stuck, and how the system sets them free.

lines.title: Cars and bays
lines.text: Think of this lot as a computer. Each car is a process, a program that wants to run. Each parking bay is a resource, like a printer or a file. A bay holds only one car at a time.

lines.title: Allocation
lines.text: Watch the cars ask for bays. The bays are free, so the system hands them out. Giving a process the resource it asks for is called allocation.

lines.title: Hold and wait
lines.text: Now car A wants to move into bay P2. But B is parked there, so A must wait. And while it waits, it keeps its own bay. This is called hold and wait.
lines.say: Now car A wants to move into bay P 2. But B is parked there, so A must wait. And while it waits, it keeps its own bay. This is called hold and wait.

lines.title: A circle of waiting
lines.text: B wants C's bay. C wants D's bay. And D wants A's bay. Every car now waits for the next one, in a circle. No one can ever move. This is a deadlock.

lines.title: Detecting the deadlock
lines.text: The system spots it by drawing who waits for whom. These arrows close into a loop, from A to B to C to D, and back to A. A loop means deadlock.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Your turn. To break the loop, the system can take a resource away by force. Select any red car, then press Tow car on the guide screen.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Let's tow car D together.

lines.title: The jam clears
lines.text: The towed car leaves and frees its bay. The next car moves in and frees another bay, and the whole jam unwinds. This is called recovery by preemption.

lines.title: Even better: avoid it
lines.text: Better still is to avoid deadlock before it happens. The Banker's Algorithm grants a request only if everyone can still finish. Try it in Banker mode. Now the lot is yours. Select a car, then a bay, and experiment.

lines.title: Welcome to Banker mode
lines.text: Welcome to Banker mode. Here you stop deadlocks before they can happen, like a careful banker who only lends money when every loan can still be paid back.

lines.title: Fleets and zones
lines.text: Each coloured fleet is a process. The two rows of bays are two types of resource: zone N in the north, and zone S in the south.

lines.title: Allocation
lines.text: Cars parked in bays show what a fleet holds right now. That is its allocation.

lines.title: Need
lines.text: Cars waiting on the street show what the fleet may still ask for, up to the maximum it declared. That is its need.

lines.title: Request and available
lines.text: The cars at the gate are a new request. Fleet A wants one more bay in zone N. The empty bays are what is still available.

lines.title: The safety check
lines.text: Before saying yes, the banker imagines granting the request. Then it checks: could every fleet still finish, one after another, using the free bays plus the bays each finished fleet gives back? If such an order exists, the state is safe, and the request can be granted.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Your turn. Look at the table, then press Grant or Deny.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Here is a hint. After granting, fleet A needs only one more bay in zone S, and one is free. So fleet A can finish first.

lines.title: Safe, well done
lines.text: Well done. After granting, fleet A can finish and return its bays, then B, then C, then D. A safe order exists, so granting was right. Watch the fleets light up in that order.

lines.title: It was safe
lines.text: Not quite. Granting was safe. After granting, fleet A can finish and return its bays, then B, C and D. Denying only made fleet A wait for nothing. Watch the fleets light up in the safe order.

lines.title: What comes next
lines.text: The next levels teach the other rules: asking for more than the declared maximum, not enough free bays, and requests that fit but are unsafe. Then try challenge mode against the clock. Press Next when you are ready.

lines.title: Welcome to the CPU lab
lines.text: Welcome to the CPU scheduling lab. A computer has only a few processor cores, but many programs that want one. Here there is a single core, and the scheduler decides who gets it next.

lines.title: Processes
lines.text: Each coloured block is a process. It needs the CPU for a number of ticks, called its burst time, and it arrives at a certain moment.

lines.title: The ready queue
lines.text: Processes that have arrived and want the CPU wait here, in the ready queue.

lines.title: The CPU core
lines.text: The core runs one process at a time. When that process finishes, or the scheduler takes the CPU away, the next one moves in.

lines.title: Scheduling algorithms
lines.text: Each desk is a scheduling algorithm: first come, first served; shortest remaining time first; priority; and round robin. Use a desk to choose one. First come, first served is selected now.
lines.say: Each desk is a scheduling algorithm: first come, first served; shortest remaining time first; priority; and round robin. Use a desk to choose one. First come, first served, is selected now.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Your turn. Start the simulation: press RUN on the console, or the RUN button.

lines.title: Hint
lines.text: Press RUN to let the scheduler start handing out the CPU.

lines.title: The Gantt chart
lines.text: Watch the timeline on the wall fill in. This is the Gantt chart: which process used the CPU, and when.

lines.title: Waiting time
lines.text: Everyone is done. A process's waiting time is the time it spent ready but not running. With first come, first served, short jobs stuck behind a long one wait a long time.

lines.title: Compare them
lines.text: Now choose another desk, run it again, and compare the waiting times. Shortest remaining time first usually waits the least, and round robin is the fairest. When you are ready, test yourself at the challenge wall.

lines.title: Welcome to the warehouse
lines.text: Welcome to the memory warehouse. A program is split into pages, but physical memory only has room for a few of them at a time.

lines.title: Frames
lines.text: The three pallets on the rack are the frames of physical memory. Each frame holds exactly one page.

lines.title: Pages
lines.text: The numbered boxes are the program's pages. The program asks for them in a fixed order, called the reference string, shown on the screen.

lines.title: Replacement policy
lines.text: When every frame is full and a new page is needed, one page must leave. The policy decides which. Let's start with FIFO: first in, first out.

lines.title: Your turn
lines.text: Your turn. Load the page the screen asks for: pick up its box, then put it on an empty pallet.

lines.title: Hint
lines.text: Look at the screen for the next page number. Pick up that box, and place it on any empty pallet.

lines.title: Page fault
lines.text: That was a page fault: the page was not in memory, so it had to be brought in. Keep loading pages in order. Soon all three frames will be full.

lines.title: Who leaves?
lines.text: Memory was full, so FIFO sent away the page that came in first. LRU would evict the page unused the longest, and Optimal the one needed furthest in the future.

lines.title: Compare the policies
lines.text: Finish the string, then try LRU and Optimal on the screen and compare the number of faults. Fewer faults means a faster program.
